title: The silkworm (fifth rooms)
hookLine: the worm spins its cocoon, dies, and a white butterfly comes out

cards: How silk is made. Teresa admits she has never seen it, only heard it told, and she tells it to her nuns anyway. A seed, tiny as a peppercorn, lies there as if dead.
When the mulberry trees leaf out in spring, it wakes up as a little worm and starts to eat. And eat. It gets fat.
Then one day it stops eating, and with its own mouth it spins silk around itself, thread by thread, until it's sealed inside a small house. Teresa marvels at it as one of the wonders of God's making.

teach.b: First, the worm is the soul. Teresa says it begins like that seed, small and not doing much, until the warmth of God wakes it up. Then it feeds: on prayer, on the sacraments, on good books and sermons.
Second, the cocoon. The house it spins, Teresa says, is Christ. She reaches for Saint Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "For you are dead; and your life is hid with Christ in God."
The soul spins by what it does: prayer, letting go of self-will, small acts of love. God does the rest. Third, the dying.
Inside the cocoon, the worm dies. That's the part that makes people wince, and Teresa doesn't soften it. The fat, busy, self-centered worm has to end.
In these fifth rooms, she says, God draws the soul into a union so close that for a short time it's hardly aware of anything else, and then it comes out changed. Fourth, the butterfly.
Out comes a little white butterfly, and Teresa is delighted by it. It's not the worm improved. It's something new.
But she adds a surprise: the butterfly is restless. It doesn't know where to land anymore. The old things it used to crawl around on don't satisfy it, and it wants God more than ever.
Teresa says that's not a problem. It's a sign. And she's honest that the change isn't always dramatic.
There's a quieter road to this union too, she says: simply wanting what God wants, day after day.

teach.h: YOUR LIFE IS HID WITH CHRIST IN GOD.
teach.b: The butterfly can be born in an ordinary life.

how: Catholic teachers often use Teresa's silkworm to describe conversion as a slow dying to self and a new life in Christ, reached by prayer, the sacraments and conforming one's will to God's in daily life.

o: a picture of clinging to your old life no matter what
a symbol of the luxuries the nuns gave up for God
Teresa's picture of dying to self and rising new in Christ

games.q: you're the silkworm. you've eaten all spring and grown fat. now something in you says: stop eating, and spin. what do you do?
o: spin the cocoon, though it means the end of you.
crawl off to find more leaves.
games.why: the worm spins its house and dies inside it, and a white butterfly comes out. Teresa says the house is Christ.

practice: Think of one small habit that belongs to the worm: a grudge you replay, a phone check you do without thinking, a need to have the last word. Just one thread; picture wrapping it up and setting it down.
If you pray, hand it to God in a sentence; if you don't, simply decide it can end.

wordCard.voice: The silkworm. Teresa's picture of the fifth rooms: the soul spins its house in Christ, dies to itself, and comes out a white butterfly. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the butterfly. The ending is how the new thing begins. Two hundred fifty days, well done.
